report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that prolonged use of cloth or surgical face masks causes dangerous carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) buildup is **false**.

Public health agencies and medical studies have thoroughly debunked this myth. Cloth and surgical masks are porous and loose-fitting, allowing gas molecules like carbon dioxide and oxygen to pass through easily. As a result, wearing these coverings does not cause hypercapnia (dangerous $\text{CO}_2$ retention in the bloodstream) or unsafe oxygen depletion.

Key evidence includes:

* **Mayo Clinic** confirms that while wearing a mask can feel warmer, the actual amount of oxygen inhaled and carbon dioxide exhaled does not change (https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/coronavirus/in-depth/coronavirus-mask/art-20485449?p=1).
* **Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)** guidance states that cloth face coverings and surgical masks do not cause harmful $\text{CO}_2$ buildup or unsafe oxygen levels for workers (https://www.safetynewsalert.com/articles/osha-cloth-masks-co2/).
* **Annals of the American Thoracic Society** published research showing that wearing surgical or cloth masks does not impair lung function or cause dangerous $\text{CO}_2$ retention, even in individuals with underlying lung diseases (https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/mask-myth-debunked-face-coverings-don-t-hurt-lung-function-n1241721).
* **Medical News Today** notes that face masks are not airtight; their breathable materials allow carbon dioxide to circulate naturally rather than build up (https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/320501).

**Sources:**
